new_statements.quote: Weak positions in metrical structure are characterized by raising and/or reduction of short vowels. Metrical structure is not a major factor in BenT in (uncompounded) noun, adjective, or numeral stems. The initial syllable is arguably a strong position, and there are many bisyllabic stems with an initial heavy syllable, e.g. bɔ̀:tɔ́ 'sack', jɛ́mbɛ́ 'bag'. However, nouns like sègérè 'filtering basket' show no phonological signs of strong and weak positions; in particular, the second syllable of a trisyllabic stem is stable. [...] So metrical structure plays a relatively small role in BenT phonology. [Sec. 2.1, p. 5:] The syllabic tones in BenT, whether lexical or grammatical, are H, L, <HL>, <LH>, and bell-shaped <LHL>.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Both daughter varieties of retired [dwl] are described as lexical/grammatical tone languages (syllable tones H, L, falling, rising, bell-shaped; every stem has at least one H; stem-wide tonosyntactic overlays). Neither grammar posits word stress or accent; the only prominence-like remark is that in Ben Tey the initial syllable is 'arguably a strong position' in a weakly developed metrical structure diagnosed by vowel raising/reduction, which Heath says plays a relatively small role. The Bankan Tey (Walo) draft leaves its 'Embryonic metrical structure' section empty and gives only the tone system (Sec. 3.7 p. 22).
new_statements.exceptions: Ben Tey verbs show final a ~ high-vowel alternations that other Dogon languages associate with weak metrical position, but Heath flags a 'cart-and-horse issue' and draws no stress conclusion; apocope of final short high vowels in CvCi stems (Sec. 3.5.3.2).
new_statements.domain_note: Statements concern stem/word-level phonology (uncompounded noun, adjective, numeral and verb stems); tone overlays are phrase-controlled (tonosyntax). No citation-form vs phrase distinction for stress because no stress is posited.
new_statements.identity_note: walo1239 / [dwl] 'Walo Kumbe Dogon' is a retired Glottolog bookkeeping languoid: ISO CR 2006-113 created [dwl] (2007) on the basis of Blench 2005; CR 2011-070 (effective 2012-02-03) split it into [dbw] Bankan Tey Dogon = Glottolog bank1259 (village Walo/Oualo, autonym bàŋkân; pop. ~1,385) and [dbt] Ben Tey Dogon = Glottolog bent1238 (Beni, Gamni, Komboy = Blench's 'Kumbe'; ~2,000-3,000). The quoted statement is from Heath's Ben Tey (Beni) grammar; the Walo-specific description is Heath's 2014 Bankan Tey draft (Sec. 3.7 p. 22, tone only). Both daughter codes already have their own check directories; any catalog entry should be filed under bank1259 and/or bent1238, not under the retired code.

sources.note: Sec. 2.1 Prosody (p.19) and 3.2.2 'Embryonic metrical structure' (p.20) are empty headings. Sec. 3.7 Tones (p.22): syllable tones H, L, R, F, <LHL>; word-final F-toned CV allowed ('this differentiates Walo from Beni'); every stem has at least one H; verbs {H}/{LH} with tone break near left edge (p.23). Words stress/accent never applied to the language.

sources.citation: Heath, Jeffrey. 2014. Dogon lexical tones of stems (cross-Dogon typological note, last update Dec 2014), 6 pp. dogonlanguages project / CDSTAR.
sources.note: Treats Bankan Tey and Ben Tey as ordinary tone languages (Bankan Tey grouped with Nanga/Togo Kan for L.H.H realization of /LH/); only Donno So is said to have moved toward a pitch accent system.
